p: Wes took the red valve out of the relief line, and the proof test will use two plugs with long red handles, and two people sign that both are out.
The real rack came down from Frederick with Irena in the cab, and its network drops were traced to a data cable shield grounded at both ends.
On the Friday before the proof test, Gus carried a bagged harness out of the cage.
It was the rack's flight power harness, W-114, and for nine days the rack had run on the stand-in's cargo wire while the as-built list said otherwise.
Brannock's fifteen year aging result on the seal is due by five that same afternoon.
Tiago Ferreira. Test lead. He's running HEARTH's proof test next week.
Wes Harland. Chief engineer. His red valve sits on the shelf over his desk.
Amara Osei. Program manager, counting the days to the proof test.
Beto Salinas. Nadia's old friend from the avionics bench. Calls her Brooks.
Helen Cho-Ramirez. Halo's crew lead. She asked what her crew does first.
Ines. Quality manager. She wants what's in the module, not the list.
Jun Takeda. Keeps the model and the verification matrix.
Tess Okonjo. Commander on Halo's first crew. She's back to live in HEARTH for a day and a half.
Chapter eleven. Test Like You Fly.

Brannock's email came in at ten to five on Friday. The long cure lot had passed its fifteen year aging test. Nadia read it, sent it on to Wes and Odette, and turned back to the harness on Tiago's desk.

The rack's flight power harness was supposed to be in the rack. The stand-in's, made of cargo wire, was there instead, and had been for nine days. The as-built list said otherwise. The proof test started Tuesday.
Monday it goes back in, Tiago said. Six o'clock. I'll be here.
Tonight it goes on the list.

She wrote the discrepancy report at his desk with her coat still on: what was installed, since when, how it got there, and that the rack had run a week of checks on a harness built for a box of ballast. At twenty to six the as-built list said so. Putting the flight harness back became a numbered step, with a check after it and two names beside it.
Tiago read it over her shoulder. It's Friday night, he said. It could've waited till Monday.
That's how it got to nine days.

Gus was in at six on Monday. Ines stood at the rack bay with the report on a clipboard while he made the swap, and she read the flight harness's label out loud before it went in. Then Tiago ran the power stage again from the top, ten percent, half, full, as if the rack had never been switched on. Every reading came up inside the band Jun had written down for it.
Wes read Brannock's email at the coffee urn with his glasses down his nose. He folded them and put them in his shirt pocket.
Good, he said. Now let's see the rest of it hold air.
Colleen's Flight Notes: test like you fly.

Colleen's new radio had passed every check on the shop's bench at Erie. On Saturday of week twenty nine she asked Nadia if she wanted to ride along on the check flight, and an hour later Nadia was in the right seat of the blue and white airplane at six thousand five hundred feet over Barr Lake, in a borrowed headset that pinched.
The shop proved it does what the box says, Colleen said. Up here I find out whether I can hear Denver approach with it.

Verification asks whether the system was built right. It gives objective evidence that an element or a system meets its specified requirements, and it happens at every level: each element against its own requirements, each subsystem against its, the whole system against the system requirements. Validation asks whether it's the right system. It gives objective evidence that the system, in use, meets the stakeholders' needs and does the job it was meant for, in the environment it was meant for. The strongest validation evidence comes from real users in realistic conditions. Validation isn't saved for the end, either: needs, concepts of operation, requirements and models can all be checked against what stakeholders really need along the way. A system can pass every verification and still fail validation, and when it does, something between the need and the evidence lost the need.

Validation takes in the stakeholder needs and requirements, the concept of operations and its scenarios, and the system or a model of it. It puts out the validation strategy, procedures and results, a validated system, and any need found unmet. That last goes back to stakeholder requirements definition or to design, and acceptance may wait on it. Human in the loop evaluations are where usability shows: real users doing real tasks, with times, errors and their own words as the data. A crew's list of what's hard to do is validation evidence even when every item on it meets spec.

How the exam asks it. Verification: against requirements, at each level. Validation: against stakeholder needs, in intended use and environment, ideally with real users. Passing one doesn't prove the other.

Clipped to her knee was a card in her small handwriting, one line per check: what, how, what counts as good, at what altitude and power. If I can't say what good looks like before I take off, she said, I'm sightseeing.

Each requirement gets a verification method: inspection, analysis, demonstration or test, plus analogy or similarity, or sampling, where those are justified. The verification matrix records, for every requirement, the method, the level where it's verified, the event or test that does it, the success criteria, the evidence, and its status. Verification is planned when requirements are written, which is one reason a requirement has to be verifiable. The process then defines procedures and the enabling systems the work needs, performs the verification, compares results with the criteria, records them, and reports anything that doesn't conform. A requirement closes when its evidence has been reviewed against its criteria and accepted, and the matrix shows that status to everyone who needs it.

Verification takes in the requirements with their verification criteria, the architecture and design, the element or system to be checked, and the enabling systems the checks need. It puts out the verification strategy and procedures, results and reports, nonconformance reports, the traceability the matrix holds, and a verified element or system. Validation uses the verified system, transition ships only what's verified, and a functional configuration audit leans on the results.
How the exam asks it. For every requirement: method, level, event, criteria, evidence, status. Closure takes objective evidence reviewed against criteria, not a test having been run.

Over the lake she switched the strobe lights on. The radio buzzed with every flash. She switched them off and the buzz went away. Strobe power supply, she said. The bench never had both of them on at once.

Test like you fly means testing in the configuration, environment and way the system will really be used. Where that isn't possible, know exactly what the test leaves out and cover it some other way. Pressure vessels get a proof test above their maximum design pressure to show the structure holds with margin and to screen out workmanship flaws, then a leak test at working pressure, because loading past working pressure can open a leak path. Thermal vacuum testing runs hardware in vacuum through its hot and cold extremes, with cycling, while it operates. Vibration and acoustic tests stand in for launch. Electromagnetic interference testing, EMI, checks what each box emits and how well it tolerates what's around it. Electromagnetic compatibility belongs to the whole system, where harnesses, grounds and every box meet, so it's verified at that level too. Qualification levels prove a design with margin. Acceptance levels screen each flight unit for workmanship without using up its life. Protoflight testing puts a flight unit through qualification levels for acceptance durations when there's no separate qualification unit.

Models get the same discipline. A model used for verification by analysis is validated itself: checked against test data for the conditions it claims to cover, with its assumptions written where its users will read them. When a test finds something a model left out, the model is corrected and every analysis that leaned on it is run again. That's how a digital thread carries a test result back to the decisions built on the old answer. A digital twin is a model kept matched to one real system and updated with that system's data through its life. Behavior lives in the model too. A sequence diagram shows the order of messages between parts over time, such as a detector, the caution system and the tone that wakes the crew.

How the exam asks it. Proof before leak. Thermal vacuum: vacuum plus temperature, while operating. EMC is a system property, verified at system level. Qualification proves the design; acceptance screens each unit.

Back on the ground she showed Nadia the top line of the card, boxed: the conditions that would end the flight on the spot, agreed before the engine started. You decide what stops you while you're still calm, she said.

A test readiness review comes before a formal test. It confirms the test article's configuration is known and controlled, procedures are approved, facilities and instruments are ready and calibrated, people are trained, hazards to people and hardware are controlled, success criteria are agreed, and every open item has been dispositioned: which ones stop the test and which can proceed as actions. Its outcome is a decision, made on stated criteria, to proceed, proceed with actions, or hold.

Quality assurance works on the project. It gives independent assurance that processes and products follow their plans, procedures and requirements: witnessing key steps, checking records and calibration, handling nonconformances, and driving root cause and corrective action, then checking the action worked. It isn't the same as quality management, the organizational process that sets the policy and system QA applies. It isn't verification either, though it watches verification closely. Its outputs, witness records, evaluation reports and nonconformance and corrective action records, feed project control and, when a cause sits in the organization's procedures, quality management.
How the exam asks it. TRR: ready to test, on stated criteria, with open items dispositioned. QA: independent, project level, witness and records, nonconformance, root cause, corrective action.
Decision one. Six hundred and twelve rows.

Monday afternoon Halo's verification lead flew in for Jun's matrix. Ines and Jun had spent the morning walking the module against the as-built list and drawings, and had found two labels turned to the wall and nothing else.

The matrix had six hundred and twelve rows, one for every requirement, derived ones included, and every row had a method. Halo's lead scrolled for ten minutes, then turned the laptop around. Forty three rows said test and nothing else. No level. No event. Nothing that said what would count as a pass.
They say test, Amara said. Tiago's going to test them. What's missing?
Every row has a method, and Halo's verification lead still turned the laptop around. What should Nadia do?
A. Give each of the forty three its level, an event and the criteria for a pass.
B. Leave the rows as they are, with the criteria held in Tiago's procedures.
C. Add pass criteria now, and fill in levels and events as each test is booked.
D. Switch the forty three to analysis, for Jun to close from the model this week.

Jun and Halo's lead take the forty three row by row. Each gets the level where it's verified, the test that does it, a number that counts as a pass, and a place for the evidence. Nine turn out to have no test planned at all. Three were going to be closed on box tests standing in for the whole module. By Wednesday every row in the matrix reads the same way, and Halo's lead stops scrolling.

That's the one. A verification matrix records, for each requirement, the method, level, event, success criteria and evidence. Without them a row can be closed by a test that ran, not by evidence that the requirement was met.

Tuesday morning Ines brought the proof procedure to the cell marked in green: five steps where quality would stand and watch before anyone went on. The calibration stickers on every gauge and transducer. Both plugs going in. The pressure hold. The strain readings. The closeout.
Tiago read her five steps and shrugged.
Ines standing there adds a day, he said. I've run every proof this cell's ever seen.
Ines has marked steps in the proof procedure where quality will watch. What should Nadia decide?
A. Count Halo's witness at the cell as the quality check for the proof.
B. Have Ines review the full data package in the days after the test is done.
C. Let Tiago sign for quality as the person who knows that cell best.
D. Keep Ines at her five witness points with her signature on each.

Nadia keeps all five of Ines's witness points. At the first one Ines checks every sticker against the calibration lab's list. One gauge on the fill panel isn't on it. It's the cell's old spare, and it gets swapped before a valve opens. She watches both plugs go in and initials each one. The test loses forty minutes, not a day.

Good. That's the call I'd sign. Quality assurance gives independent assurance that work follows its plans and that the evidence is objective. Witnessing key steps, checking calibration and signing apart from the doers are core QA.

The nitrogen ran into HEARTH all Tuesday night. Proof came first on Wednesday morning, because pushing a shell past its working pressure is what opens a leak if one is waiting, and the leak test is there to find it afterward. Wes stood in the cell until Tiago sent him out, then stood at the window with his palm flat on the glass.

The pressure went up in steps and held. The strain gauges climbed, held, and came back to zero on the way down. Then twenty four hours at working pressure, corrected for the cell's temperature. Thursday afternoon Jun put the number up. A third of the allowable leak rate.
Both relief ports still had the ground plugs in them, long red handles and all. The two flight relief valves sat on Tiago's bench with their bench test tags.
Close it, Wes said. Those plugs seal tighter than any valve.
The leak test read a third of allowable, with ground plugs in both relief ports. When should it close?
A. Close it with the valves bolted on, on the strength of their bench tests.
B. Close it on Thursday's number, with the plugs noted as tighter than valves.
C. Close the module's leak row now, with a new row for the relief valves alone.
D. Close it once the valves are back on and leak checked right where they sit.

Nadia keeps the row open until the valves are checked where they sit. They go back on Friday. Gus adds a trace of helium to the fill and checks each flange with a sniffer while the module holds pressure, and both come in clean. The closure record names Thursday's run, the plugs that were in for it, and Friday's two checks, so the evidence covers exactly what will fly.

Exactly right. Verification evidence counts for the configuration tested. When the test article differs from flight, the difference is recorded and covered by another check, so the flight configuration itself is verified.

In week thirty the flight forward hatch rode up the highway to Longmont on a flatbed, wrapped like furniture, to a thermal vacuum chamber FRO had rented for a week. Its seals came from Brannock's long cure lot. Tiago's fixture held cabin pressure on one side, as HEARTH would, and vacuum on the other. Wes rode up in the truck.
The qualification hatch had held air at room temperature in week eighteen. Nothing of this design had been cold in vacuum yet.
Amara had the chamber's day rate on her phone. The seal just passed fifteen years of aging, she said. Do we need two days of cold soak on top of that?
In Longmont, the flight forward hatch sits in a rented thermal vacuum chamber. How should the test run?
A. Drop the cold soak, with the aging result standing in for it.
B. Measure the leak hot and cold, working the latches at each plateau.
C. Run the cycles in the chamber, then measure leak once at room temperature.
D. Cycle it in FRO's own oven in air, with the chamber days given back.

At the cold plateau the leak rate climbs to about two thirds of the allowable, then settles back as the hatch warms. The latches take more force cold, still inside what a crew can pull. Every number goes in the record. Cold rubber's stiff, Wes says, reading it. Now we know how stiff. They stay through the second night. At two in the morning the chamber hums, the plots crawl, and there's nothing to do but watch them. Wes has his glasses up on his head and a coffee from the vending machine he isn't drinking. Your dad, he says, out of nowhere. Gus says he read every tag on the valve panel. He did. Lineman? Thirty one years. Wes nods at the plot, where the leak line has started to bend back down. Tell him the door held cold, he says. He'll ask how cold. Then tell him that too.

That's the one. Thermal vacuum testing verifies function and performance in vacuum across the temperature extremes, while operating. Test like you fly: measure and operate the hardware the way it will be used, at the conditions it will see.

On Friday of week thirty her own row closed. Tiago held a calibrated smoke source under the cabin sensor in the main air return above the galley, and the alarm went at four seconds, with sixty allowed. Ines read the record and signed the closure. Fire detection, verified by test. Nadia felt the small click, and this time she didn't argue with it.

Saturday she drove to Colorado Springs. FRO had rented a day in her old shop's EMI chamber, the electromagnetic interference room where boxes get tested for electrical noise, for HEARTH's power distribution unit, and Beto Salinas, her old bench partner, was running it from the same chair, with the same bad coffee. The box passed emissions and susceptibility in every band. He saw her laptop open to the matrix and leaned over.

Look at that. Green. He grinned. You still love a green PASS, Brooks. She told him her own row had closed the day before, fire detection, four seconds. He clinked his bad coffee against hers. Bench is the easy part, he said. Call me when somebody's slept in it.

Then her phone went. Amara, from home. Halo wanted the module's electromagnetic compatibility requirement, EMC, closed on today's result. Noisiest box aboard just passed, she said. Can I tell them it's done?
Saturday's EMI run passed the power distribution unit in every band. What should that result close?
A. Close the module's EMC row by analysis, adding up the results of every box's test.
B. Close it on integration, where HEARTH ran all week without a network drop.
C. Close the box's rows today, with the module's EMC row left for a module test.
D. Close the module's EMC row on this box's result, the noisiest one aboard.

The box's rows close that afternoon. The module's EMC row goes into the integrated test, with every box, the rack, the fans and every harness running, and the station radio frequencies watched. Beto hears about the ground loop from week twenty seven and laughs. That's the one, he says. Box tests never see that one.

Good. That's the call I'd sign. Requirements are verified at the level where they're specified. Element results support a system requirement like EMC, but closing it takes evidence from the integrated system, where the interactions live.

Monday of week thirty one Helen called. Halo was sending Commander Tess Okonjo back, with three of her crew, on Wednesday for the human-in-the-loop evaluation: thirty six hours living in HEARTH on the high bay floor, then the emergency runs, ending Thursday night with the sleep period fire Helen had written in herself.
Halo's verification lead was at Nadia's desk with the matrix open on her laptop when the call ended.
Six hundred rows, she said, almost all closed or booked. She wanted to know what a crew was going to tell them that the matrix couldn't.
Halo is sending Commander Tess Okonjo and three crew for the evaluation. Who should run the scenarios, and how?
A. Have FRO's engineers run the scenarios, as the people who know the module.
B. Have Halo's trainers run the scenarios, with the crew watching from outside.
C. Count the verification results as validation, with each requirement traced to a need.
D. Have Halo's crew live in it and run every scenario from their own bunks at night.

Tess's crew will come in flight clothes. They'll eat, sleep and work in HEARTH for thirty six hours with the module's real procedures, then run every emergency scenario from their own bunks. Jun writes down what Halo needs to see from each run, need by need, before the first one starts.

Exactly right. Validation shows the system meets stakeholder needs in its intended use and environment. The strongest evidence comes from representative users doing real tasks in realistic conditions.

Tess Okonjo came in Wednesday morning with a duffel bag and three crew, and asked to walk the module before anyone briefed her. She'd walked it on tape and lain in it in plywood. This was the first time it had a ceiling. Nadia took her down the aisle. Past the galley, Tess stopped between quarters three and four and looked at both.
Nadia knew the numbers. One. By the hatch.

Good answer. Tess dropped her duffel into four, the far quarter. Last one out is the commander's. She took a photo out of her jacket, two boys on a dock holding one small fish between them, and taped it to the wall beside the pillow. They like to know where I sleep. Forty grams, Nadia thought. She'd left them on the sheet.

They lived in HEARTH through Wednesday and the night after. Thursday morning Tess handed Nadia a clipboard with twenty seven items on it in pencil. The galley table blocked the aisle when it was down. The hatch handle's cover caught a glove. The hygiene station's door swung out into the path. None of them failed a requirement. Amara read the list over Nadia's shoulder.
Every one of these meets spec, she said.
Tess hands Nadia twenty seven items from a day and a half in HEARTH. What should happen to them?
A. Close them as out of scope, with HEARTH meeting every requirement.
B. Fix all twenty seven before ship, with nothing left on the crew's list.
C. Trace each to the need it touches, then settle it with Halo's crew office.
D. Fix the ones Tess ranked highest, with the rest put on the sustaining list.

Jun and Helen sit with Tess's list all afternoon. Each item gets the need it touches and how much it matters. Four become design changes, nine become procedure changes, and fourteen are accepted as they are, with a reason Tess signs. The galley table gets a latch that won't let it stay down across the aisle.
That's the one. Validation findings are recorded, traced to the stakeholder needs they affect, and resolved with the stakeholder: a change, a procedure, or accepted with rationale.

Thursday at ten the lights went out in HEARTH. Four crew in four bunks, curtains drawn. Odette had the stop button. Helen sat at Tiago's console in a headset, watching four screens, one particle counter for each quarter, hung where the crew's heads would be because she had asked for them there. In the aft hatch a duct fan stood in for the air Halo's node would push through on orbit. Behind the hygiene station's panel Tiago's generator waited to put out tracer smoke where a fan motor might burn.
It started at fourteen past. The cabin sensor would alarm, the crew would wake, and Jun's stopwatch would run from there.

The counters in one, two and three stayed flat. Four climbed. The cabin sensor's trace gave one small bump, nowhere near its alarm, and went flat again. Tess had asked for a tone that kept going until somebody answered it. Nothing had started one. At three minutes quarter four's counter crossed the level that would have set the sensor off. Odette looked over at Helen. Helen shook her head. It's tracer. I want to see if it finds her. At five it was twice that. Odette's hand was over the button.
At six minutes four's curtain moved. Tiago, Tess said from the dark, in a perfectly ordinary voice. Is this supposed to be in here? Odette stopped the run.

Somebody hit the work lights. Nadia went down the aisle. Tess was sitting up on the edge of bunk four in her socks with the stuff still all around her, gray, from the ceiling down to a hand off the pillow. It smelled sweet, like the fog machine at a high school dance. In the aisle you could see where the duct fan pulled: clean air, galley to aft hatch, one straight shot. Four's opening sat half behind the hygiene wall, out of it. With the curtain shut, the air just went on by. Her boys were still taped up by the pillow, them and their one fish, gone soft in the gray.

Helen had got as far as the galley, headset still on, the cord swinging where she'd pulled it out of the console. She was looking at the curtain. I asked for the curtains, she said. So they'd hear the alarm.
Amara had come down behind Helen. She looked at the pillow, and put her phone back in her pocket.
The sensor passed. It was out before Nadia could stop it. I closed that row. Four seconds.
Tiago had the camera up. He let it down, and he didn't say it unkindly. At the detector, he said. Nobody sleeps at the detector.

Ernie at the switch with his tester, saying dead on the radio. Her under the galley vent watching Tiago's smoke can, typing PASS. Dad had been a mile down the road. Tess had been down the aisle with her boys on the wall.
The tracer pooled in quarter four while the cabin sensor barely moved. What should Nadia do now?
A. Move the cabin sensor toward quarter four tonight, then run it again.
B. Leave the module as it stands, then trace the failure back to its start.
C. Record it as outside the requirement, which the cabin sensor met.
D. Rerun it tomorrow night with the same setup, then write it up for Halo.

No one touches the curtain. Tiago photographs the quarter and saves every counter's data. That night Nadia and Jun trace it back. The requirement said detect smoke anywhere in the habitable volume within sixty seconds. The verification point said the cabin sensor. The hazard report's detection control cited that sensor's test. The requirement had been right. The place she had proved it hadn't.

Good. That's the call I'd sign. A validation failure means the system doesn't meet the need in real use even though its requirements were recorded as verified. Keep the evidence, record it, and trace back through requirements, verification and hazard controls to find where the need was lost.
Decision nine. What kind of problem.
She called her sister Callie from the car in the lot at a quarter to one. Callie was on nights. She picked up on the second ring, and the first thing she said was Who's hurt?
No one. No one's hurt. Then she told it, badly and out of order. The tracer. The counter. Quarter four. The photo on the wall. I gave the call, Cal. I said dead, and they went to bed under it.
The line was quiet long enough that Nadia looked at the screen to see if she'd lost her.
No. She found it. The commander. She sleeps in it.
Then your crew tested where they touch, Callie said. That's the whole thing. It's never one call, and yours was one call.
You said that at the sink.
I said a lot of things at the sink.

A radio went off behind her, somebody wanting a switching order. Hang on. She keyed it. Nadia listened to her sister read the order out, then sit through the crew lead reading the whole thing back, then ask him where he was going to test it, and wait till he said. Go ahead. She came back on. Sorry.
Don't be. That's the first of three. You don't give Ernie's call. I knew that at the sink, and I said it anyway. I'm sorry.

Well, I'm sorry about twice a year, Callie said. It's one in the morning and you called me first, so I'm counting it. The radio again. She let it go a second. You were right too. One check is one check. I just hate it when you're the one saying it.
Somebody did leave one in, a few weeks back. Nine days.
Don't make it a thing. I'm not telling Dad till you've had your big review. Go to bed.

Friday Jun ran the smoke model again with the curtain in it. The assumption page from the trade still said what it had said then: the cabin modeled as one open volume, fans at nominal. The curtain had never been in it. With one, the model put a pocket in quarter four inside three minutes. He ran it again with gravity off, as on orbit, where nothing rises and only the fans move smoke. The pocket was still there.

He didn't say much when he showed her. He'd printed the assumption page and put it on her desk with a pencil box around one line. I wrote that in week ten, he said. One open volume. It was on page two the whole time.
I read page two, Nadia said. So did everybody at the trade.

And it found the pocket in an afternoon, once somebody told it about the curtain. She slid the page back across the desk. Put Thursday in it. Every counter, every run. Then it's checked against the module instead of against us. By that night the model carried the counters from the crew run beside its own curves, the curtain in its geometry, and a new line on page two with the date and his initials.
Ines came up from quality at ten with the drawings under her arm. Every part in that module matches its drawing, she said. So tell me what kind of problem this is.
Jun's model now shows the curtain pocket even with gravity off. How should the finding be handled?
A. Change the design through the board, verify the change, and close the finding.
B. Write a nonconformance against the cabin sensor and send it to the review board.
C. Change the design through the board, and have Ines find why verification missed it.
D. Close it as no defect, with the hardware built and installed to every drawing.

The change request puts a detector in every quarter at the head of the bunk, the station's standard unit. Halo has four in its spares and can ship them in week thirty four. Ines opens a corrective action on FRO's verification planning. The root cause is hers to write: verification points for hazard controls were chosen for how testable they were, and no one checked them against where the crew would be in each scenario. Now every one gets that check. She reruns it on all forty hazard reports, and two more points move. She'll check the next program's matrix herself.

Exactly right. Nothing in the module was built wrong, so there's no hardware nonconformance to disposition. The gap is in the design and the verification plan. The design changes through change control, and QA drives root cause and corrective action on the process that let it through, then checks that the fix worked.

Jun's verification status review with Halo and OCSC, the federal office that audits human rating, was Monday at nine: three hours, every open row. Every review Jun had given so far, Nadia had been in the room for.
Friday afternoon Amara stopped at her desk. Nadia had the detector change, the hazard report and Odette for the whole week ahead. Do you want to take Monday yourself, Amara asked, or push it?
Jun was two desks over and heard it. He didn't look up. Later, at the urn, he asked her straight out. Will you be on the line?
Jun's verification status review is Monday at nine, and Nadia's week is full. What role should she take?
A. Let Jun run it alone, with what he can commit to agreed first.
B. Let Jun run it, with her dialed in on mute, ready to step in if needed.
C. Run it herself this time, with Jun taking notes beside her as before.
D. Push the review a week for her to sit beside him one more time.

Nadia tells Jun the review is his. They spend twenty minutes Friday on what he can agree to in the room and what comes back to her. Monday she's in quarter four with Odette and a tape measure, her phone in her desk drawer. OCSC's observer asks to close thirty rows on cargo heritage. Jun takes them one at a time, agrees to eleven where the conditions match, and says no to nineteen with reasons. Afterward he finds her at quarter four. I'd bring up the fire row myself next time, he says. I waited to be asked. He'd said no nineteen times, and he doesn't mention it.
That's the one. Developing people means real responsibility with clear limits, room to do the work without being rescued, and reflection after. Competency grows through practice, not observation.

Thursday night Colleen met her at the diner on Arapahoe Road and ordered pie for both of them without asking. She listened to all of it: quarter four, the photo, what Tiago said about the detector. She didn't say any of the things Nadia had braced for. She cut a corner off her pie and left it on the plate.

I owe you a story about a colonel. She set her fork down. I was a captain, she said. Night before a deployment move, a jet came out of maintenance, and on the engine run it felt wrong. Not a number. A feel, through the seat. Every gauge in the green. My colonel wanted it on the ramp by morning, and he asked me if I had anything besides a feeling. I didn't. So I flew it.

It came back. Everybody shook my hand. She turned her coffee cup a little. Coming back isn't the same as being right. I've known that a long time. I never found out if anything was wrong with that jet. What I know is I had a room where I could have said no, and I said yes, because I couldn't prove it.
Then you've got it easier than I did, Colleen said. You still have to say it. She picked up the check. I told you something in a booth like this once. About gates.

Friday morning Amara put the open items for the test readiness review, the TRR, on the HEARTH room screen. Twenty three of them, from the detector change to a procedure redline nobody had signed. The integrated acceptance test started Monday afternoon if the review said so.
Which of these stop Monday? Amara asked.
Twenty three open items sit on the TRR list. What should Nadia do with them?
A. Hold the test until all twenty three are closed, with not one going in open.
B. Write the blocking criteria first, then sort all twenty three against them.
C. Ask each item's owner whether theirs blocks, then sort on their answers.
D. Take all twenty three in as open items, to be closed while the test runs.

Nadia writes the blocking criteria at the top of the list before anyone sorts: could it hurt someone, change what's being tested, or spoil a result. Amara's name and Odette's go under them. Four items meet one: the detectors that aren't in yet, a software build not yet released, the unsigned redline, and one transducer past its calibration date. The other nineteen go in as actions, each with an owner and a date. Every call gets one line of reason.

Good. That's the call I'd sign. Decision management sets the criteria before judging the options, so the decision is consistent and on record. A TRR decides on stated criteria which open items block the test and which can proceed as actions.

Sunday at eight she called Pueblo. Callie put Rosie on, and Rosie held the rocket up to the camera with its green door open until her arm got tired. Their father was out back in the tomatoes, Callie said, and gave her a look that said that was on purpose.

Then Nadia opened the TRR package. Jun had built it from the matrix. The fire detection row had read the same since Friday of week thirty: verified by test, closed, PASS, N. Brooks. The detector change sat in its own section as a finding from the crew evaluation, with Odette's hazard report beside it. Nothing in the package said who had picked the cabin sensor, or why.
After the Sunday call to Pueblo, Nadia opens the TRR package. What should she do about her row?
A. Reopen her own row in red, with her name and her reasoning written under it.
B. Leave the row closed, and show the detectors as an addition to the design.
C. Report it as a test finding with the fix and dates, leaving out whose call it was.
D. Put it down to the smoke model, which had one volume and no curtain.

She writes one page. The row goes red and says reopened. Under it: the point she chose in the architecture work, why she chose it, what it missed in quarter four, and every other row she verified the same way, which she's checking herself before Monday. She sends it to Jun and Amara at eleven, so neither of them sees it first in the room.
Exactly right. SE ethics asks for honesty and accountability: disclose your own errors promptly to the people relying on your work, and own the correction.

The TRR started at eight on Monday of week thirty three in the big conference room off the lobby, the one with the lighting company's old logo still etched in the glass. Helen and Ken Mallory, Halo's program manager. The OCSC observer. Ines, Odette, Wes, Tiago, and Amara in the chair. Colleen came in late and took a seat by the wall.

Jun walked the matrix. He did it as he had the Monday before, and didn't look at Nadia once. Six hundred and twelve rows. Twenty three open items: four that held their part of the test, nineteen going in as actions with owners and dates.
Then the fire detection row came up on the screen. It said reopened, in red, with her name in the owner column and her page under it.

I picked the cabin sensor as the verification point for fire detection, she said. Back when we built the architecture. I picked it because all the cabin air comes back there, and because it was easy to test, and because I knew it would pass. It passed. In the crew run Commander Okonjo lay in quarter four with smoke a hand off her pillow, and it never went off.
The requirement was right. Detect smoke anywhere in the habitable volume. I verified it in one place, the place it would pass. That gap is mine. Not the model's, and not the curtain's.
She looked at the back wall. Colleen hadn't moved.

A gate is where you're allowed to say we're not ready, Nadia said. Fire detection isn't ready. It said ready from week thirty on, because I signed it. Hold its part of the test until there's a detector in every quarter and we've proved each one at the pillow, curtain shut, from every source in every scenario.

Amara didn't poll the room. Proceed on everything else, she said. Fire detection holds, and the fire hazard report reopens with it. Nadia owns the verification. Odette owns the hazard. She wrote it into the minutes herself, and for once she didn't ask what it would cost.
Helen caught Nadia at the door afterward. Tess asked me to tell you something, she said. She's keeping four.
Her phone rang at seven that night while she was still in the lot. Dad, the screen said. He never called on a Monday.
Your sister says you two are talking, he said. Says you had a couple of weeks.
She told him. All of it, in order this time, as she'd told the room. The tracer. Quarter four. The photo. Tiago. The sensor she'd picked because it would pass. He let her get all the way to the end.
I did Ernie's job, she said. Tested it at the switch and called it dead.
Ernie checked it right, he said. Sounds like you did too. That curtain wasn't on you, any more than that fella's generator was on him.
Don't. It came out harder than she meant. You can give Ernie that. He didn't pick the switch. I picked the sensor, Dad. I picked it because it would pass.
There was only the traffic on Arapahoe for a while, through the windshield.
Okay, he said. Then it's yours.

It's mine, she said, and since they were there anyway, she asked him for the other half. Why he'd never told her. He'd given her half of it out in the tomatoes, on one knee, and she'd driven home with it.

Other half's worse, he said. Every class I ever had, I was the fella who climbed it. A room full of guys every year looking at my hand and knowing why. With you I was just your dad who got hurt. She heard him breathe out. I liked being that. I wasn't in any hurry to trade it.

She didn't have an answer for that, and he didn't seem to want one. Somebody on Arapahoe laid on a horn for no reason she could see. Then he asked about the picture. Where'd the commander put it. By her pillow, Nadia said. Scotch tape. Crooked.
Leave it up when you test it, he said.
